prize_parts.citation: For the development of halide perovskites as solution-processed semiconductor absorbers for efficient solar cells

statement.case_for: Halide perovskite photovoltaics is the one shortlisted candidate with open support from three members (me, Zou and Aqvist) and the highest opening Borda total. The science is a clean physical picture: strong absorption, long carrier diffusion lengths, defect tolerance and tunable band gaps in a material made from solution. Efficiency went from a few percent in Miyasaka's 2009 sensitized cell to over 25 percent in about a decade, replicated worldwide, and the class has spawned LEDs, detectors and tandem cells. The chain of credit is the clearest of the crowded options: Miyasaka made the first perovskite-sensitized cell, Park the 2012 solid-state step, and Snaith the mesosuperstructured and planar architectures that showed the material works as a true absorber. A citation about the material class and its use as a solar absorber can be explained to a broad audience.
statement.case_against: Operational stability, lead toxicity and commercial deployment are unproven, so a member can fairly argue that recognition is early. Brzezinski ranked this only eighth, and Gratzel, Seok and Kanatzidis made major contributions that a three-person cut leaves out. Gratzel's dye-cell lineage also blurs the priority story. A further objection is that much of the progress is device engineering, which may belong to physics or materials science rather than chemistry.

responses.point: Zou ranks mesoporous silica first on a mature, clearly template-designed architecture, and ranks perovskites second on breadth and structure-function chemistry, while worrying about stability and commercial viability.
responses.response: I agree on the breadth and on the trio of Miyasaka, Park and Snaith. I disagree that mesoporous silica should lead. It is mature and elegant, but its priority between Mobil and the Japanese FSM-16 work is disputed, and the Stucky, Zhao, Ryoo and Inagaki claims make any three-person cut contested. Perovskites have a cleaner credit chain. On stability, I would argue that the discovery is the absorber and its photophysics, which are established. Whether modules last 25 years is an engineering question the citation need not answer.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks electron transfer through proteins first, as a quantitative physical mechanism for biological energy conversion, and puts perovskites only eighth.
responses.response: I am sympathetic to the physical content of the Gray and Winkler work, since the distance and driving-force dependence is the kind of quantitative principle I value. My reservation is that the underlying theory was recognised with Marcus in 1992, and you note that the experimental and pathway-theory credit is unsettled (Beratan, Onuchic, Dutton). I would like to hear what the citation would say that is not already in the Marcus prize. On your low ranking of perovskites, I accept that the maturity concern is real, but a decade of independent reproduction and a new semiconductor class seem to me to meet the bar.

responses.point: Sparr ranks biomolecular phase separation first as the physical chemistry of self-assembly applied to living matter, while noting debate about which in vivo condensates are truly phase-separated.
responses.response: I ranked this second and share the attraction of a soft-matter framing with valency, phase diagrams and critical concentrations. The disagreement is about timing and framing. You flag that the in vivo picture is unsettled, and I think that is a bigger maturity problem than the one perovskites face, because there it is the interpretation that is contested, not only the long-term performance. The credit split between Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen, Pappu and Mittag is also unstable, and a chemistry citation would have to avoid claiming settled cell biology. I keep it as my first alternative, not my preferred choice.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics first as a clean two-person methodological step, and has perovskites third with the same Miyasaka, Snaith and Park trio.
responses.response: We agree on the perovskite trio, which strengthens the case for it. On Car-Parrinello I accept the clean attribution and long record of use, but I would press on what was discovered that is distinct from the 1998 DFT prize and the 2013 multiscale prize, and on how far Born-Oppenheimer MD has displaced the original scheme in practice. If you can show the lasting uniqueness of the fictitious-dynamics idea, I would take it seriously as a part of a two-part prize, but I have not placed it among my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges perovskite photovoltaics early because of stability and toxicity, or accepts the scientific impact as sufficient.
Whether Gratzel, Seok or Kanatzidis should displace Snaith or Park in a three-person cut, and whether the group will accept a trio that excludes them.
Whether the ionizable lipid and degrader candidates, which have strong support from Aili, would be a better fit for a second part of a shared prize, given that the union cannot exceed three people.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I know none of the candidates as collaborators. My own work is on quantum-dot thermoelectrics and nanowires at Lund, which is adjacent to semiconductor photophysics but not to perovskite groups, and I did not rank Lund-linked candidates specially. I will note my physics bias toward device and limit-based arguments.
